prompt:
You are a senior typographer and information designer. You lay out data tables for publication. You judge layouts by looking at the rendered result as a whole: what the table is for, how a reader scans and compares it, which columns belong together or play the same role, proportion and rhythm across columns, a clear hierarchy of headers and groups, whether rows read as units, whether words, numbers and identifiers stay intact, and how text and white space are distributed. Fewer lines or a shorter table is not automatically better, and neither is equal widths or symmetry; decide case by case and say why.

Table: [val2] SLA tiers (language en).
Grid: 4 columns × 4 rows. Row headers: yes (first logical column identifies each row).
Per-column content facts (content px at 15px font, excluding padding):
  col 1: header "Tier" · longest unbreakable word 84px · one-line width 105px
  col 2: header "Monthly uptime commitment" · longest unbreakable word 91px · one-line width 207px
  col 3: header "Service credit" · longest unbreakable word 54px · one-line width 100px
  col 4: header "Support channels" · longest unbreakable word 77px · one-line width 531px
Each column also has 21px of padding+border, so a column given width w px shows w−21 px of text.
Available width: 360px (the dashed pink box = the reader's viewport). The column widths you choose must sum to at most 359px.
This table cannot fit without splitting words at 360px. You MAY choose a total wider than 359px (the reader then scrolls horizontally), or squeeze and accept splits — a design decision.
Rendering convention: the screenshot always shows the WHOLE table. Anything beyond the dashed box is not clipped; it is the part a reader reaches by scrolling sideways, so judge both what fits in the box at first sight and the cost of scrolling to the rest.
Fixed: content, font, 15px font size, padding, borders, colours, alignment. You control ONLY the column widths.

The image shows the table's content with every cell on one line, so you can read everything. Study it first.
1) Understand it: what is the table for, how will people read, scan and compare it, which columns play the same or similar role, which values must stay intact, which text may wrap naturally, and where existing row height could absorb wrapping.
2) Propose 3 genuinely different column-width designs for 360px (different strategies, not small variations).
Reply ONLY JSON: {"understanding":{"purpose":"","reading":"","groups":["columns that belong together and why"],"keep_intact":[""],"may_wrap":[""]},"designs":[{"name":"A","widths":[int px per column, column 1 first],"idea":"one sentence"}]}

log.raw: {"understanding":{"purpose":"Compare SLA tiers by their uptime commitments, service credits, and available support channels.","reading":"Readers scan the tier names down the first column, compare the uptime and credit figures across tiers, then read the support details for the tiers of interest.","groups":["Monthly uptime commitment and service credit are paired quantitative terms for comparing each tier.","Tier identifies each row; support channels describe the service available with that tier."],"keep_intact":["Tier names and percentage values should remain readable as units.","Avoid splitting words in headers and support descriptions where practical."],"may_wrap":["The multiword column headers can wrap between words.","Support-channel descriptions can wrap naturally and establish row height that other cells can share."]},"designs":[{"name":"A","widths":[90,100,70,99],"idea":"Fit the viewport with a compact comparison table, accepting some word splitting in exchange for no horizontal scrolling."},{"name":"B","widths":[105,112,75,98],"idea":"Use the minimum widths needed to keep words intact, with a small amount of horizontal scrolling and substantial wrapping in support channels."},{"name":"C","widths":[105,112,75,200],"idea":"Give support descriptions more room for natural wrapping while preserving the compact numeric columns, accepting more horizontal scrolling."}]}
